items.title: Shakespeare coined or first-recorded around 1,700 English words
items.claim: Many words first attested in Shakespeare are still common. Which of these did he first put on paper?

options.text: Eyeball, bedroom, lonely, swagger, gossip and assassination
Only obscure words found in Hamlet's longer speeches
No words — Samuel Johnson coined them in 1755

items.reveal:
OED first-citation counts vary by scholar (around 1,700, often disputed because earlier sources may have been lost). Words first attested in Shakespeare include eyeball (Tempest), bedroom (Midsummer Night's Dream), lonely (Coriolanus), swagger (Midsummer Night's Dream), gossip (used as a verb meaning to chatter), assassination (Macbeth), bandit (Henry VI), and zany (Love's Labour's Lost).

Many are first uses on paper of words that may have been spoken; some are genuine inventions; some are repurposings (verb from noun and vice versa).
items.why: 'The author of half your vocabulary' is a tagline, but it points to something real: literature isn't a passive record of language, it actively shapes it.

items.title: Jane Austen never put her name on her novels in her lifetime
items.claim: Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park and Emma were published while Austen was alive. How were they credited?

options.text: Under her own name from the start
Anonymously — 'By a Lady' for Sense and Sensibility, then 'By the Author of...' for subsequent novels

items.reveal:
Sense and Sensibility (1811) was published 'By a Lady'. Pride and Prejudice (1813) was 'By the Author of Sense and Sensibility', and so on. Authorship was an open secret in literary London — Henry Austen leaked it — but never appeared on the title page.

After her death in 1817, her brother Henry's biographical notice attached to Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817-18) named her publicly.

Female novelists publishing under their own names was not impossible (Fanny Burney did) but carried social cost. Anonymity was a respectable middle path for a clergyman's daughter.
items.why: The literary fame we grant Austen retrospectively obscures how invisible female authorship often was. Authorship itself has a history.

items.title: The novel as a form is only about 300 years old in English
items.claim: Tragedy, epic poetry and lyric are ancient. When did the English novel emerge as a recognisable form?

options.text: Around 1700 BCE, with the Epic of Gilgamesh
In the late 17th and early 18th centuries — Aphra Behn's Oroonoko (1688), Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719), Richardson's Pamela (1740)
With Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in the 14th century

items.reveal:
Ian Watt's 'The Rise of the Novel' (1957) traced the English novel to Defoe, Richardson and Fielding, linking it to the rise of the middle class, print capitalism and Protestant interiority. Earlier prose narratives existed (Don Quixote, 1605; Genji, 11th century) but the realist, character-centred novel in English coalesces around 1700-1750.

The Greek and Latin canons had long prose works (Petronius's Satyricon, Heliodorus's Aethiopica) but these are episodic and rhetorical, not novelistic in Watt's sense.

Novels were initially considered a low, suspect form — read by women, dangerous to morals.
items.why: Treating 'literature' as a timeless category hides the fact that the novel itself is a modernity-shaped form. Its conventions (free indirect discourse, the omniscient narrator, the bildungsroman) emerged with the bourgeoisie.
